claims.source: By contrast, the loss of Hri1 and Hri2, two other eIF2α kinases in S. pombe (Zhan et al., 2004), did not affect autophagy after leucine starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F and a citation.

claims.claim: Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
claims.source: By contrast, the loss of Hri1 and Hri2, two other eIF2α kinases in S. pombe (Zhan et al., 2004), did not affect autophagy after leucine starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F), indicating that Gcn2 exclusively regulates the leucine starvation-induced autophagy among the S. pombe eIF2α kinases.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of effect of Hri1 and Hri2 deletion on leucine starvation-induced autophagy.

claims.claim: The Gcn2 kinase forms a complex with the Gcn1 and Gcn20 proteins that facilitate activation of Gcn2.
claims.source: The Gcn2 kinase forms a complex with the Gcn1 and Gcn20 proteins that facilitate activation of Gcn2 (Garcia-Barrio et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Autophagy in response to leucine starvation was abrogated by the gcn1∆, but not gcn20∆, mutation.
claims.source: Autophagy in response to leucine starvation was abrogated by the gcn1∆, but not gcn20∆, mutation (Figure 4D), consistent with the fact that Gcn1 directly regulates Gcn2, but Gcn20 has only a minor role in Gcn2 signaling (Sattlegger et al., 2004; Yuan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D and citations.

claims.claim: Autophagy after leucine starvation was severely impaired in cells lacking Cpc2 and in those overexpressing a fission yeast ortholog of Yih1/IMPACT.
claims.source: We found that autophagy after leucine starvation was severely impaired in cells lacking Cpc2 and in those overexpressing a fission yeast ortholog of Yih1/IMPACT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), confirming the essential role of the Gcn2 activity in autophagy induction upon amino acid starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: The eIF2α-S52A strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.source: In order to test whether the Gcn2 kinase induces autophagy through phosphorylation of eIF2α, we constructed a strain that expresses eIF2α with its phosphorylation site Ser52 substituted by alanine (eIF2α-S52A). The strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 4E), indicating the critical role of the eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2 plays a critical role in leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.source: In order to test whether the Gcn2 kinase induces autophagy through phosphorylation of eIF2α, we constructed a strain that expresses eIF2α with its phosphorylation site Ser52 substituted by alanine (eIF2α-S52A). The strain was defective in the leucine starvation-induced autophagy (Figure 4E), indicating the critical role of the eIF2α phosphorylation by Gcn2.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the autophagy defect in the eIF2α-S52A mutant.

claims.claim: After leucine starvation, the Fil1 protein increased, which was dependent on Gcn2 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed that, after leucine starvation, the Fil1 protein increased, which was dependent on Gcn2 and the phosphorylation of eIF2α (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: S. pombe cells lacking Gcn3 or Fil1 displayed autophagy defects during leucine starvation.
claims.source: Moreover, S. pombe cells lacking Gcn3 (Figure 4D) or Fil1 (Figure 4F) displayed autophagy defects during leucine starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 4D and 4F.

claims.claim: Activation of the transcriptional program induced by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway promotes autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
claims.source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that activation of the transcriptional program induced by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway promotes autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence showing the requirement of Gcn2, eIF2α phosphorylation, and Fil1 for autophagy.

claims.claim: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable.
claims.source: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable, indicating that TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation.
claims.source: When fission yeast cells were starved of leucine, the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 became undetectable, indicating that TORC1 activity is suppressed upon leucine starvation (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of Psk1 phosphorylation during leucine starvation.

claims.claim: Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after leucine starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains.
claims.source: In contrast, Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after the starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains (Figure 5A), suggesting that TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
claims.source: In contrast, Psk1 remained phosphorylated even after the starvation in the gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ mutant strains (Figure 5A), suggesting that TORC1 inactivation in leucine-starved cells is mediated by the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of Psk1 phosphorylation in Gcn2 pathway mutants.

claims.claim: The autophagy defect of the gcn2∆ mutant was complemented by TORC1 inactivation by the TORC1 inhibitors, rapamycin and caffeine.
claims.source: Moreover, the autophagy defect of the gcn2∆ mutant was complemented by TORC1 inactivation by the TORC1 inhibitors, rapamycin and caffeine (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The Gcn2 pathway attenuates TORC1 activity in response to amino acid starvation to induce autophagy.
claims.source: These results suggest that the Gcn2 pathway attenuates TORC1 activity in response to amino acid starvation to induce autophagy.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the rescue of gcn2∆ autophagy defect by TORC1 inhibitors.

claims.claim: The strains lacking the functional TSC or GATOR1 complex showed no apparent defect in amino acid starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.source: In stark contrast to the Gcn2 pathway mutants, the strains lacking the functional TSC or GATOR1 complex showed no apparent defect in amino acid starvation-induced autophagy; free GFP, the product of the autophagic degradation of Pgk1-GFP, accumulated after leucine starvation even in the tsc2∆ iml1∆ double mutant (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Amino acid starvation can induce autophagy independent of the TSC and GATOR1 complexes.
claims.source: Thus, amino acid starvation can induce autophagy independent of the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, two important negative regulators of TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal autophagy in tsc2∆ iml1∆ cells during leucine starvation.

claims.claim: Significant autophagy induction was observed in gcn2∆, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ cells incubated in the growth medium with no nitrogen source.
claims.source: On the other hand, we observed significant autophagy induction in gcn2∆ (Figure 5D), eIF2α-S52A, and fil1∆ (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) cells incubated in the growth medium with no nitrogen source.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Nitrogen depletion triggered TORC1 inactivation in Gcn2 pathway mutants as in the wild-type strain.
claims.source: Consistently, nitrogen depletion triggered TORC1 inactivation in these Gcn2 pathway mutants as in the wild-type strain (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The Gcn2 signaling pathway appears to be specifically responsible for induction of autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
claims.source: Therefore, the Gcn2 signaling pathway appears to be specifically responsible for induction of autophagy in response to amino acid starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential requirement of Gcn2 for autophagy during amino acid versus nitrogen starvation.

claims.claim: The Gcn2-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α and the Fil1 expression increased more significantly during starvation for leucine than that for nitrogen.
claims.source: Such a specific role of the Gcn2 pathway during amino acid starvation is also congruous with our observation that the Gcn2-dependent phosphorylation of eIF2α and the Fil1 expression increased more significantly during starvation for leucine than that for nitrogen (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: In the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double-mutant cells starved of nitrogen, autophagy was severely reduced and delayed, in comparison to those in the wild-type and individual single-mutant cells.
claims.source: In the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double-mutant cells starved of nitrogen, autophagy was severely reduced and delayed, in comparison to those in the wild-type and individual single-mutant cells (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant.
claims.source: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant (Figure 6B,C), implying that GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.source: The autophagy defect in the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant was even more severe than that in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ double mutant (Figure 6B,C), implying that GATOR1 and Gcn2 are two main contributors to the nitrogen starvation-induced autophagy.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of autophagy defects in different double mutants.

claims.claim: In the gnc2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant, a trace of released GFP was detected only after 14 hr of nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: In the gnc2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant, a trace of released GFP was detected only after 14 hr of nitrogen starvation (Figure 6C), while autophagy takes place within 2 hr in wild-type cells after the starvation (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Autophagy induction upon nitrogen starvation is dependent on the three negative regulators of TORC1 signaling, GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex.
claims.source: These data indicate that autophagy induction upon nitrogen starvation is dependent on the three negative regulators of TORC1 signaling, GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the severe autophagy defect in the triple mutant.

claims.claim: In strains lacking GATOR1, Gcn2, and the TSC complex, severely impaired suppression of TORC1 activity during nitrogen starvation was confirmed by monitoring the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1.
claims.source: Not surprisingly, in strains lacking these regulators, severely impaired suppression of TORC1 activity during nitrogen starvation was confirmed by monitoring the TORC1-dependent phosphorylation of Psk1 (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant exhibited a significant delay in the nitrogen starvation-responsive TORC1 inactivation.
claims.source: Especially, the gcn2∆ iml1∆ double mutant exhibited a significant delay in the nitrogen starvation-responsive TORC1 inactivation, consistent with its severe defect in autophagy induction (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant showed robust Psk1 phosphorylation even after 12 hr of nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: With a more severe autophagy phenotype (Figure 6C), the gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant showed robust Psk1 phosphorylation even after 12 hr of nitrogen starvation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type.
claims.source: Indeed, nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B); the loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: The loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
claims.source: Indeed, nitrogen starvation provoked significant eIF2α phosphorylation in the GATOR1- and TSC-defective strains, but not in the wild type (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B); the loss of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes may be compensated by activation of the Gcn2 kinase to attenuate TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased eIF2α phosphorylation in GATOR1 and TSC mutants.

claims.claim: Nitrogen starvation induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells.
claims.source: Nitrogen starvation also induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), implying that autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: Nitrogen starvation also induced significant Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants, such as atg7∆ and isp6∆, more than in wild-type cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), implying that autophagy suppresses Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the increased Gcn2 activation in autophagy-defective mutants.

claims.claim: Reduced autophagy in the absence of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes after nitrogen starvation may lead to intracellular amino acid depletion, which induces Gcn2 activation via uncharged tRNAs.
claims.source: It is plausible that reduced autophagy in the absence of the GATOR1 and TSC complexes after nitrogen starvation (Figure 4A) may lead to intracellular amino acid depletion, which induces Gcn2 activation via uncharged tRNAs (Wek et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the relationship between autophagy and Gcn2 activation, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Autophagy became detectable 2–3 hr after nitrogen starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ strain.
claims.source: Autophagy became detectable 2–3 hr after nitrogen starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ strain, and much later in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, while gcn2∆ iml1∆ cells showed only minuscule autophagy signals even after 9 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The reduction in TORC1 activity was observed early after the starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ mutant, followed by the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, and then the gcn2∆ iml1∆ strain.
claims.source: Consistently, the reduction in TORC1 activity, as judged by Psk1 dephosphorylation, was also observed early after the starvation in the iml1∆ tsc2∆ mutant, followed by the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant, and then the gcn2∆ iml1∆ strain (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: Gcn2 signaling contributes the most to TORC1 attenuation during nitrogen starvation, whereas the TSC complex does the least among the three.
claims.source: These observations may reflect the contributions of the three negative regulators of TORC1 during nitrogen starvation; Gcn2 signaling contributes the most, whereas the TSC complex does the least among the three.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the kinetics of autophagy and TORC1 inactivation in different mutants.

claims.claim: The gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant with functional GATOR1 exhibited a transient reduction in TORC1 activity within 1 hr of nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: Of note, the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant with functional GATOR1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,F), but not the gcn2∆ iml1∆ tsc2∆ triple mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2F), exhibited a transient reduction in TORC1 activity within 1 hr of nitrogen starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E and F.

claims.claim: GATOR1 can attenuate TORC1 promptly after nitrogen starvation, but negative feedback regulation that re-activates TORC1 or inhibits GATOR1 might be induced in response to the TORC1 attenuation.
claims.source: Therefore, it seems that GATOR1 can attenuate TORC1 promptly after the starvation, but negative feedback regulation that re-activates TORC1 or inhibits GATOR1 might be induced in response to the TORC1 attenuation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the transient TORC1 inactivation in the gcn2∆ tsc2∆ mutant.

claims.claim: The GATOR1-dependent TORC1 attenuation preceded the Gcn2-mediated TORC1 inhibition, which became apparent after 2 hr of nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: This GATOR1-dependent TORC1 attenuation preceded the Gcn2-mediated TORC1 inhibition, which became apparent after 2 hr of the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Together with GATOR1, the TSC complex may be able to initiate the suppression of TORC1 activity much earlier than the Gcn2 pathway after nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: In addition, in the gcn2∆ single mutant that retains both GATOR1 and the TSC complex, a notable reduction in TORC1 activity was observed even earlier, within 10 min after the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G). Thus, together with GATOR1, the TSC complex may be able to initiate the suppression of TORC1 activity much earlier than the Gcn2 pathway after nitrogen starvation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the early TORC1 inactivation in the gcn2∆ mutant.

claims.claim: The relatively late contribution of Gcn2 to TORC1 attenuation in starved cells can be explained by the fact that Gcn2 functions through the Fil1-mediated transcriptional events.
claims.source: The relatively late contribution of Gcn2 to TORC1 attenuation in starved cells can be explained by the fact that Gcn2 functions through the Fil1-mediated transcriptional events.
claims.evidence: The claim is an inference based on the mechanism of Gcn2 action.

claims.claim: eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 up-regulation were detectable as early as at 15 min after nitrogen starvation.
claims.source: Indeed, eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 up-regulation were detectable as early as at 15 min after the starvation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2H), whereas the Gcn2-dependent TORC1 inactivation took place after 2 hr and later (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2H.

claims.claim: The tsc1∆ and tsc2∆ mutants show no apparent growth defect, but introduction of the gcn2∆ mutation to them resulted in a detectable growth defect.
claims.source: The tsc1∆ and tsc2∆ mutants show no apparent growth defect, but introduction of the gcn2∆ mutation to them resulted in a detectable growth defect (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: The gcn2∆ mutation exacerbated the growth defects in cells lacking functional GATOR1 or Sea3.
claims.source: In addition, the gcn2∆ mutation exacerbated the growth defects in cells lacking functional GATOR1 (Figure 6G) or Sea3 (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claims.claim: Not only gcn2∆ but also fil1∆ exhibited similar synthetic growth defects when combined with the tsc2∆ or sea3∆ mutation.
claims.source: Not only gcn2∆ but also fil1∆ exhibited similar synthetic growth defects when combined with the tsc2∆ (Figure 6I) or sea3∆ (Figure 6J) mutation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6I and 6J.

claims.claim: Growth phenotypes caused by the Gcn2 pathway mutations combined with the loss of the other negative regulators of TORC1 were largely suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium or by the any1∆ mutation.
claims.source: Importantly, these growth phenotypes caused by the Gcn2 pathway mutations combined with the loss of the other negative regulators of TORC1 were largely suppressed by rapamycin in the growth medium (right panels in Figure 6F–J) or by the any1∆ mutation (Figure 6K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figures 6F-K.

claims.claim: Along with the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, the Gcn2 signaling pathway also contributes to TORC1 attenuation in the presence of ample nutrients.
claims.source: Thus, it is likely that, along with the TSC and GATOR1 complexes, the Gcn2 signaling pathway also contributes to TORC1 attenuation in the presence of ample nutrients.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the synthetic growth defects and their suppression by rapamycin or any1∆.

claims.claim: iml1∆ and tsc2∆ cells starved of nitrogen gradually lost viability.
claims.source: We also noticed that iml1∆ and tsc2∆ cells starved of nitrogen gradually lost viability, though such a phenotype was not detectable with the gcn2∆ mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Significantly reduced mating and sporulation were observed in strains carrying the iml1∆ mutation.
claims.source: Significantly reduced mating and sporulation were observed in strains carrying the iml1∆ mutation, suggesting an important role of GATOR1 in the induction of sexual differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mating and sporulation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: GATOR1 plays an important role in the induction of sexual differentiation.
claims.source: Significantly reduced mating and sporulation were observed in strains carrying the iml1∆ mutation, suggesting an important role of GATOR1 in the induction of sexual differentiation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduced mating and sporulation in iml1∆ mutants.

claims.claim: The iml1∆ defect in sexual differentiation was exacerbated in combination with the gcn2∆ or tsc2∆ mutation.
claims.source: The iml1∆ defect was exacerbated in combination with the gcn2∆ or tsc2∆ mutation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mating and sporulation assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: The negative regulators of TORC1 are required for proper starvation responses, such as cell survival and sexual differentiation, in fission yeast.
claims.source: These observations indicate that the negative regulators of TORC1 are required for proper starvation responses, such as cell survival and sexual differentiation, in fission yeast.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the viability and sexual differentiation defects in mutants lacking TORC1 regulators.

claims.claim: Under nutrient-rich conditions and during starvation, fission yeast TORC1 is negatively regulated by the TSC complex, the Gcn2 signaling pathway, and GATOR1, which requires the presumed GATOR2 component Sea3 for its full function.
claims.source: In summary, under nutrient-rich conditions and during starvation, fission yeast TORC1 is negatively regulated by the TSC complex, the Gcn2 signaling pathway, and GATOR1, which requires the presumed GATOR2 component Sea3 for its full function (Figure 6L).
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claims.claim: In mammalian cells, two classes of Ras-related small GTPases, Rheb and the Rag, serve as key regulators of mTORC1 activation.
claims.source: In mammalian cells, two classes of Ras-related small GTPases, Rheb and the Rag, serve as key regulators of mTORC1 activation (González and Hall, 2017; Wolfson and Sabatini, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The TSC and GATOR1 complexes harbor GAP activity toward Rheb and RagA/B, respectively.
claims.source: The TSC and GATOR1 complexes harbor GAP activity toward Rheb and RagA/B, respectively, and control these GTPases to negatively regulate mTORC1 activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Growth factors and nutrient signals induce mTORC1 activation by suppressing the GAP function of the TSC and GATOR1 complexes to promote anabolism and restrain autophagy.
claims.source: Growth factors and nutrient signals induce mTORC1 activation by suppressing the GAP function of these complexes to promote anabolism and restrain autophagy.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The GATOR1 and TSC complexes attenuate TORC1 activity not only during nitrogen starvation but also under nutrient-rich conditions in fission yeast.
claims.source: We previously identified the GATOR1 complex in fission yeast and showed that the GATOR1 and TSC complexes attenuate TORC1 activity not only during nitrogen starvation but also under nutrient-rich conditions (Chia et al., 2017; Fukuda and Shiozaki, 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claims.claim: Mammalian GATOR2 is inhibitory to GATOR1, promoting mTORC1 activation in the presence of amino acids.
claims.source: It has been reported that mammalian GATOR2 is inhibitory to GATOR1, promoting mTORC1 activation in the presence of amino acids (Bar-Peled et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The predicted molecular architecture of the SEA complex, a GATOR equivalent in budding yeast, suggests that Sea3 serves as an interaction hub among the constituting subunits.
claims.source: The predicted molecular architecture of the SEA complex, a GATOR equivalent in budding yeast, suggests that Sea3 also serves as an interaction hub among the constituting subunits (Algret et al., 2014), though the sea3∆ mutation has little impact on TORC1 activity in this organism (Panchaud et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: The sea3∆ mutation has little impact on TORC1 activity in budding yeast.
claims.source: The predicted molecular architecture of the SEA complex, a GATOR equivalent in budding yeast, suggests that Sea3 also serves as an interaction hub among the constituting subunits (Algret et al., 2014), though the sea3∆ mutation has little impact on TORC1 activity in this organism (Panchaud et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: S. pombe Sea3 is not required for the integrity or vacuolar localization of GATOR1, but promotes the GAP function of GATOR1 by enhancing the interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase.
claims.source: We found that S. pombe Sea3 is not required for the integrity or vacuolar localization of GATOR1, but promotes the GAP function of GATOR1 by enhancing the interaction between GATOR1 and the Gtr1 GTPase.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: Gcn2, an eIF2α kinase conserved among eukaryotes, is activated by uncharged tRNAs that accumulate in amino acid-starved cells.
claims.source: Gcn2, an eIF2α kinase conserved among eukaryotes, is activated by uncharged tRNAs that accumulate in amino acid-starved cells (Wek et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α inactivates translation initiation in general, while enhancing that of specific mRNAs encoding certain transcription factors, such as budding yeast Gcn4, mammalian ATF4, and fission yeast Fil1.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α inactivates translation initiation in general, while enhancing that of specific mRNAs encoding certain transcription factors, such as budding yeast Gcn4, mammalian ATF4, and fission yeast Fil1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: In fission yeast, Gcn2 senses lack of different amino acids and induces autophagy through inhibition of TORC1.
claims.source: Our study has revealed that, in fission yeast, Gcn2 senses lack of different amino acids and induces autophagy through inhibition of TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α followed by an increase in Fil1 is involved in the Gcn2-mediated autophagy induction.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α followed by an increase in Fil1 is also involved in the Gcn2-mediated autophagy induction, indicating that the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway mediates amino acid starvation signals to negatively regulate TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the requirement of eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 for autophagy.

claims.claim: The Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway mediates amino acid starvation signals to negatively regulate TORC1.
claims.source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α followed by an increase in Fil1 is also involved in the Gcn2-mediated autophagy induction, indicating that the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway mediates amino acid starvation signals to negatively regulate TORC1.
claims.evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Fission yeast Gcn2 was previously proposed to function downstream of TORC1 because inactivation of TORC1 stimulates Gcn2 kinase.
claims.source: It should be noted that fission yeast Gcn2 was previously proposed to function downstream of TORC1 because inactivation of TORC1 stimulates Gcn2 kinase (Valbuena et al., 2012).

results.result: All five subunits of mammalian GATOR2 (Sea2, Sea3, Sea4, Sec13, Seh1) are conserved in fission yeast and form a complex with GATOR1 to constitute the GATOR holocomplex.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1B) identifying all five GATOR2 orthologs and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1C) demonstrating their physical interaction with GATOR1. The identification of Sea2 through improved purification completes the conservation of all five mammalian GATOR2 subunits.

results.result: GATOR1 and most GATOR2 subunits (Sea2, Sea3, Sea4, Seh1) localize to vacuolar membranes in fission yeast, while Sec13 shows predominantly nuclear and cortical localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C48 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data (Figures 1D-H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing vacuolar localization of GATOR1 and GATOR2 subunits. The observation that Sec13 localizes primarily to nuclear periphery and cell cortex (consistent with its known roles in nuclear pore complex and COPII) suggests only a small fraction participates in GATOR2.

results.result: Loss of Sea3, but not other GATOR2 subunits, results in growth defects suppressible by rapamycin, indicating deregulated TORC1 activation and a distinctive role for Sea3 in negative regulation of TORC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 2A) showing that sea3Δ exhibits growth defects both alone and in combination with other GATOR2 deletions, and that rapamycin suppresses this defect. This phenotype is unique among GATOR2 components and implicates Sea3 in TORC1 inhibition.

results.result: Loss of Any1 rescues the growth defects of sea3Δ and iml1Δ mutants, suggesting Sea3 and GATOR1 suppress deregulated TORC1 activation that impedes amino acid uptake.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 2B) and citation to previous work. The any1Δ suppression phenotype is consistent with the model that Sea3 and GATOR1 prevent TORC1 hyperactivation that inhibits amino acid permease localization.

results.result: Sea3 functions in the same pathway as GATOR1 but in parallel to the TSC complex to attenuate TORC1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by genetic epistasis analysis (Figures 2C-D). The lack of additive growth defects between sea3Δ and GATOR1 mutations indicates they function in the same pathway, while synthetic growth defects with TSC mutations (suppressible by rapamycin) demonstrate parallel pathways.

results.result: Expression of GDP-locked Gtr1 (gtr1S16N) suppresses the sea3Δ growth defect, suggesting Sea3 is required for GATOR1's GAP activity toward Gtr1.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 2E). The genetic suppression by GDP-locked Gtr1 is consistent with the model that Sea3 promotes GATOR1's function as a GAP for Gtr1, as GDP-locked Gtr1 bypasses the need for GAP activity.

results.result: Sea3 is required for prompt TORC1 inactivation upon nitrogen starvation, as monitored by Psk1 dephosphorylation, though GATOR1 retains partial activity in sea3Δ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 2F-G) showing delayed Psk1 dephosphorylation in sea3Δ cells compared to wild-type, but less severe delay than in iml1Δ cells. The other GATOR2 components show normal Psk1 dephosphorylation kinetics.

results.result: Sea3 mediates the physical interaction between GATOR1 and other GATOR2 components (Seh1, Sea2, Sea4, Sec13), and Sea3 can bind GATOR1 independently of these other GATOR2 subunits.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figures 3A-E) showing that Sea3 is required for GATOR1-GATOR2 interactions, but Sea3-GATOR1 interaction persists in the absence of other GATOR2 components. This suggests Sea3 directly binds GATOR1 and serves as a bridge to other GATOR2 subunits.

results.result: Sea3 binding to GATOR1 requires an intact GATOR1 complex, and Sea3 localizes to vacuolar membranes through its interaction with GATOR1.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation (Figures 3F-H) and fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) showing that deletion of any GATOR1 subunit disrupts Sea3-GATOR1 interaction and causes Sea3 to diffuse throughout the cytosol rather than localizing to vacuoles.

results.result: Deregulated TORC1 activation per se does not cause Sea3 cytosolic diffusion, as Sea3 remains vacuolar in cells expressing GTP-locked Gtr1Q61L.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 is supported by fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) showing vacuolar Sea3 localization in gtr1QL cells despite TORC1 hyperactivation. This control demonstrates that Sea3 mislocalization in GATOR1 mutants is due to loss of GATOR1 interaction, not secondary effects of TORC1 deregulation.

results.result: Sea3 is essential for vacuolar localization of other GATOR2 components (Sea2, Sea4, Seh1) and plays an essential role in GATOR holocomplex assembly on the vacuolar surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E) showing that Sea2, Sea4, and Seh1 lose vacuolar localization in sea3Δ cells. Combined with interaction data, this supports Sea3's role as a scaffold mediating GATOR2 assembly with GATOR1 on vacuoles.

results.result: Sea3 is not essential for GATOR1 complex integrity or vacuolar localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 are supported by immunoblotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), co-immunoprecipitation (Figures 3J-L), and fluorescence microscopy data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-G) showing that GATOR1 subunits maintain normal protein levels, pairwise interactions, and vacuolar localization in sea3Δ cells.

results.result: Sea3 enhances the physical interaction between GATOR1 and Gtr1 GTPase, potentially facilitating GATOR1's GAP function.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 3M) showing reduced Iml1-Gtr1 interaction in sea3Δ cells. While the mechanism is speculative (C78 uses 'raises the possibility'), the reduced interaction provides a plausible explanation for Sea3's role in promoting GATOR1 GAP activity.

results.result: Arg98 of Npr2, but not Arg854 of Iml1, acts as an arginine finger essential for GATOR1 GAP activity in fission yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 are supported by growth assay data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,C) showing that iml1R854A has no growth defect while npr2R98A exhibits compromised growth rescued by rapamycin or GDP-locked Gtr1. This corrects previous work and aligns with recent mammalian GATOR1 structural studies.

results.result: Autophagy is partially reduced but still detectable in tsc2Δ iml1Δ double mutants during nitrogen starvation, indicating an additional TORC1 attenuation mechanism beyond GATOR1 and TSC.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by Pgk1-GFP processing assay data (Figure 4A) showing residual autophagy in tsc2Δ iml1Δ cells. This observation motivates the search for additional TORC1 regulators and leads to identification of the Gcn2 pathway.

results.result: Leucine starvation induces autophagy in fission yeast in a Gcn2-dependent manner, as evidenced by Gcn2 activation (eIF2α phosphorylation) and GFP accumulation from Pgk1-GFP processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 4B-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) showing eIF2α phosphorylation and GFP accumulation during leucine starvation in wild-type but not gcn2Δ cells. This establishes Gcn2 as essential for amino acid starvation-induced autophagy.

results.result: Gcn2-dependent autophagy can be induced by starvation of various amino acids (leucine, arginine, histidine, glutamine) in fission yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-E) showing Gcn2-dependent GFP accumulation during arginine starvation and treatment with 3-AT (histidine biosynthesis inhibitor) or MSX (glutamine biosynthesis inhibitor). This demonstrates broad amino acid sensing by Gcn2.

results.result: Gcn2 exclusively regulates leucine starvation-induced autophagy among S. pombe eIF2α kinases, as Hri1 and Hri2 deletion has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) showing normal autophagy in hri1Δ and hri2Δ cells during leucine starvation. This specificity establishes Gcn2 as the dedicated amino acid starvation sensor among eIF2α kinases.

results.result: Gcn2 complex components Gcn1 (but not Gcn20) and regulators Cpc2 and Yih1/IMPACT are required for leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G) showing autophagy defects in gcn1Δ, cpc2Δ, and yih1-overexpressing cells, but not gcn20Δ cells. This is consistent with known Gcn2 regulation mechanisms.

results.result: The Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 transcriptional pathway promotes autophagy in response to amino acid starvation, as eIF2α-S52A, gcn3Δ, and fil1Δ mutants are defective in leucine starvation-induced autophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 4E-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H) showing that eIF2α phosphorylation, Fil1 upregulation, and the downstream transcription factor Fil1 are all required for autophagy during leucine starvation. This establishes the complete Gcn2 signaling pathway.

results.result: TORC1 activity (monitored by Psk1 phosphorylation) is suppressed upon leucine starvation through the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 5A) showing loss of Psk1 phosphorylation during leucine starvation in wild-type cells but persistent phosphorylation in gcn2Δ, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1Δ mutants. This links Gcn2 signaling to TORC1 inhibition.

results.result: The Gcn2 pathway attenuates TORC1 to induce autophagy, as TORC1 inhibitors (rapamycin, caffeine) rescue the autophagy defect of gcn2Δ mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 5B) showing that rapamycin and caffeine restore autophagy in gcn2Δ cells during leucine starvation. This demonstrates that Gcn2's role in autophagy is mediated through TORC1 inhibition.

results.result: Amino acid starvation induces autophagy independent of TSC and GATOR1 complexes, as tsc2Δ iml1Δ double mutants show normal autophagy during leucine starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 5C) showing GFP accumulation in tsc2Δ iml1Δ cells during leucine starvation. This contrasts with the requirement for Gcn2 and demonstrates pathway specificity.

results.result: The Gcn2 pathway is specifically responsible for autophagy induction during amino acid starvation but not nitrogen starvation, as Gcn2 pathway mutants show normal autophagy and TORC1 inactivation during nitrogen starvation.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 5D-E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) showing significant autophagy and TORC1 inactivation in gcn2Δ, eIF2α-S52A, and fil1Δ cells during nitrogen starvation. This establishes stimulus-specific roles for different TORC1 regulatory pathways.

results.result: Gcn2-dependent eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 expression increase more during leucine starvation than nitrogen starvation.
results.evaluation: Claim C119 is supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 5F) comparing eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 levels during leucine versus nitrogen starvation. This biochemical observation is consistent with the differential requirement for Gcn2 in these two starvation conditions.

results.result: Autophagy induction upon nitrogen starvation depends on three parallel negative regulators of TORC1: GATOR1, Gcn2, and TSC complex, with GATOR1 and Gcn2 being the main contributors.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C124 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 6A-C) showing progressively more severe autophagy defects in gcn2Δ tsc2Δ, gcn2Δ iml1Δ, and gcn2Δ iml1Δ tsc2Δ mutants. The triple mutant shows only trace autophagy after 14 hours, demonstrating the combined requirement for all three pathways.

results.result: TORC1 activity suppression during nitrogen starvation is severely impaired in strains lacking GATOR1, Gcn2, and TSC, as monitored by Psk1 phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C127 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figures 6D-E) showing delayed or absent Psk1 dephosphorylation in double and triple mutants, with the gcn2Δ iml1Δ tsc2Δ triple mutant showing robust Psk1 phosphorylation even after 12 hours. This confirms the parallel pathways converge on TORC1.

results.result: Loss of GATOR1 and TSC complexes leads to compensatory Gcn2 activation during nitrogen starvation, possibly due to reduced autophagy causing intracellular amino acid depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C) showing increased eIF2α phosphorylation in GATOR1/TSC mutants and autophagy-defective mutants during nitrogen starvation. However, the proposed mechanism (C129, C132) is speculative and lacks direct experimental validation. The compensatory activation is observed but the causal chain remains uncertain.

results.result: Among the three TORC1 regulators during nitrogen starvation, Gcn2 contributes most to TORC1 attenuation, followed by GATOR1, then TSC complex, based on kinetics of autophagy and TORC1 inactivation in double mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-D) showing differential timing of autophagy induction and Psk1 dephosphorylation in iml1Δ tsc2Δ (earliest), gcn2Δ tsc2Δ (intermediate), and gcn2Δ iml1Δ (latest) mutants. This kinetic analysis reveals the relative contributions of each pathway.

results.result: GATOR1 and TSC complex can initiate rapid TORC1 suppression within 10-60 minutes of nitrogen starvation, preceding Gcn2-mediated inhibition (after 2 hours), though GATOR1 may be subject to negative feedback regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E-G) showing transient TORC1 inactivation in gcn2Δ tsc2Δ cells and early inactivation in gcn2Δ cells. The negative feedback hypothesis (C137) is speculative but consistent with the transient nature of GATOR1-mediated inhibition. The temporal separation of pathways is well-documented.

results.result: The late contribution of Gcn2 to TORC1 attenuation (after 2 hours) is explained by its requirement for Fil1-mediated transcription, though eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 upregulation occur within 15 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are supported by immunoblotting data (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E,H) showing early eIF2α phosphorylation and Fil1 upregulation (15 min) but delayed TORC1 inactivation (2+ hours). The lag between transcription factor activation and TORC1 inhibition is consistent with a transcriptional mechanism.

results.result: The Gcn2 pathway contributes to TORC1 attenuation under nutrient-rich conditions, as gcn2Δ or fil1Δ mutations cause synthetic growth defects with tsc2Δ or sea3Δ that are suppressible by rapamycin or any1Δ.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are supported by growth assay data (Figures 6F-K) showing synthetic growth defects in double mutants combining Gcn2 pathway mutations with TSC or GATOR1 pathway mutations, and suppression by rapamycin or any1Δ. This demonstrates that Gcn2 contributes to basal TORC1 regulation even without starvation.

results.result: TORC1 negative regulators (GATOR1, TSC, Gcn2) are required for proper starvation responses including cell survival and sexual differentiation in fission yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 are supported by viability assay data (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) and mating/sporulation assay data (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B) showing reduced viability in iml1Δ and tsc2Δ cells during prolonged nitrogen starvation, and severely reduced sexual differentiation in iml1Δ cells (exacerbated by gcn2Δ or tsc2Δ). This demonstrates physiological importance beyond growth regulation.

results.result: Sea3, a fission yeast ortholog of mammalian GATOR2 subunit WDR59, is physically and functionally proximal to GATOR1 rather than GATOR2, promoting GATOR1's GAP function to attenuate TORC1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4 and C65 represent the central finding of the paper. They are supported by: (1) sequence homology establishing Sea3 as WDR59 ortholog; (2) genetic data showing sea3Δ phenocopies GATOR1 mutants (Figures 2A-E); (3) biochemical data showing Sea3 mediates GATOR1-GATOR2 interaction and enhances GATOR1-Gtr1 binding (Figures 3A-M); (4) functional data showing Sea3 is required for efficient TORC1 suppression (Figures 2F-G). This is a major conceptual advance showing GATOR2 component functions with GATOR1.

results.result: The fission yeast GATOR complex is dispensable for TORC1 regulation during amino acid starvation, which instead activates the Gcn2-eIF2α-Fil1 pathway to inhibit TORC1 and induce autophagy.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C163-C165 represent a major finding. They are supported by: (1) normal autophagy in tsc2Δ iml1Δ cells during leucine starvation (Figure 5C); (2) complete dependence on Gcn2, eIF2α phosphorylation, and Fil1 for autophagy during amino acid starvation (Figures 4C-F, 5A); (3) rescue of gcn2Δ autophagy defect by TORC1 inhibitors (Figure 5B). This establishes a novel, GATOR-independent mechanism for amino acid sensing.

results.result: Nitrogen starvation suppresses TORC1 through combined actions of GATOR1-Sea3 complex, Gcn2 pathway, and TSC complex, implementing multiple parallel signaling pathways for proper cellular starvation responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 and C152 represent the integrative conclusion. They are supported by: (1) severe autophagy defects only in triple mutants (Figure 6C); (2) impaired TORC1 suppression in double and triple mutants (Figures 6D-E); (3) synthetic growth defects and sexual differentiation defects in double mutants (Figures 6F-K, Figure 6—figure supplement 3). The parallel pathway model is well-supported by genetic and biochemical data.

results.result: TORC1 inactivation during amino acid starvation is exclusively mediated by Gcn2, while nitrogen starvation induces swift TORC1 inactivation primarily through GATOR1 and TSC, with Gcn2 playing a cryptic compensatory role.
results.evaluation: Claims C178-C184 synthesize the stimulus-specific regulation. They are supported by: (1) exclusive Gcn2 requirement for amino acid starvation responses (Figures 5A-C); (2) normal TORC1 inactivation in Gcn2 mutants during nitrogen starvation (Figure 5E); (3) rapid TORC1 inactivation kinetics during nitrogen versus amino acid starvation (Figure 5F); (4) compensatory Gcn2 activation in GATOR1/TSC mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The speculation about mechanism (C181) is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Fission yeast lacks Sestrins and CASTOR1, using the Gcn2 pathway instead for amino acid sensing, while the mechanisms by which GATOR1 and TSC sense nitrogen remain unknown, illustrating organism-specific choreography of conserved TORC1 regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C189 provide evolutionary context. C186-C187 are supported by the functional data showing Gcn2-dependent responses to leucine and arginine starvation (Figures 4-5) in the absence of Sestrin/CASTOR1 orthologs. C188 is a knowledge statement. C189 is a well-supported inference from the comparative data showing different pathway utilization across species despite conservation of core components.
